sn54.1:1.7: For _parimukhaṁ_ (“present”) we find _pratimukha_ in Sanskrit, which can mean “presence” or the reflection of the face. Late canonical Pali explains _parimukhaṁ_ as “the tip of the nose or the reflection of the face (_mukhanimitta_)”. _Parimukha_ in Sanskrit is rare, but it appears in Pāṇini 4.4.29, which the commentary illustrates with the example of a servant “in the presence” of their master (cp. [sn47.8]()). So it seems the sense is “before the face” or more generally “in the presence”. | To “bring mindfulness” (_satiṁ upaṭṭhapetvā_) is literally to “do satipaṭṭhāna”. The root sense of _upaṭṭhāna_ is to “stand near” or “attend” (like a nurse on a patient, [sn47.13:1.3]()), and the Sanskrit _upasthāna_ is commonly used in the sense “homage” of the gods, based on the idea of “attending” the sacred flame. A literal translation of the phrase might be, “having made memory attend to what is present”.
